title: Mindscape × Sean Carroll — 原子大部分是空的吗？物理学家至今说不准
title_en: Mindscape × Sean Carroll — Are atoms mostly empty space? Physicists still can't say

questions.question: 按 Sean Carroll 的讲法，原子里电子的能量为什么只能取一组离散的值？
options: 因为自然在最底层就是像素化的，空间和能量本来就一格一格，量子力学只是如实反映了这一点
因为每次测量都会扰动电子，把它推到某个固定的能级上，不测量时能量本来是任意的
薛定谔方程本身是连续的，离散来自边界条件，就像两端钉住的吉他弦
因为玻尔规定了电子只能待在某些轨道上，这条规定至今仍是量子力学的基本公设
questions.explanation: Carroll 强调量子性不是因为自然本身离散，而是在盒子里或原子核附近解波动方程时，得到的解恰好是一组离散解；自由空间里的电子可以有任何能量。「自然本来就是像素化的」正是他明确否定的误读。
questions.question_en: On Sean Carroll's account, why can an electron in an atom only take a discrete set of energies?
options_en: Nature is pixelated at bottom, with space and energy coming in chunks, and quantum mechanics simply reflects that
Every measurement disturbs the electron and knocks it onto a fixed level; unmeasured, its energy could be anything
The Schrödinger equation is continuous; discreteness comes from boundary conditions, like a guitar string pinned at both ends
Bohr decreed that electrons may occupy only certain orbits, and that rule remains a basic postulate of quantum mechanics
questions.explanation_en: Carroll stresses that quantumness doesn't come from nature being fundamentally discrete; solving the wave equation in a box or near a nucleus just happens to yield a discrete set of solutions, while a free electron can have any energy. "Nature is pixelated" is the very misreading he rejects.

questions.question: 教科书（哥本哈根）诠释给出了测量时的三条规则：结果总是确定的、概率按玻恩规则算、测后波函数坍缩。Carroll 说的「测量问题」指的是什么？
options: 这些规则只在「测量」时启用，而什么算测量从未被定义：眼睛、摄像机、猫、单个原子算不算都说不清
测量时人的意识会直接改变波函数，而意识的物理机制尚未被找到
玻恩规则算出的概率和实验数据对不上，说明这三条规则本身有错
测量仪器的精度有限，永远无法同时精确测出电子的位置和动量
questions.explanation: Carroll 说这三条规则在教科书里都有，本身没有争议，争议在于理论另加了一整套只在「测量」时启用的规则，却从没说清测量是什么。说规则和实验对不上是错的：它们预测得很好，问题出在定义而不是数据。
questions.question_en: The textbook (Copenhagen) interpretation gives three rules for measurement: you always get a definite result, probabilities follow the Born rule, and the wave function collapses afterward. What does Carroll mean by the "measurement problem"?
options_en: These rules kick in only during a "measurement," yet what counts as one has never been defined—an eye, a camera, a cat, a single atom?
A human mind directly alters the wave function during measurement, and the physical mechanism of mind hasn't been found
The probabilities from the Born rule don't match experimental data, showing the three rules are wrong
Instruments have limited precision, so an electron's position and momentum can never both be measured exactly
questions.explanation_en: Carroll says the three rules are in every textbook and uncontroversial as such; the trouble is that the theory bolts on a separate set of rules for "measurement" without ever saying what measurement is. Claiming the rules clash with experiment is wrong—they predict superbly; the problem is definitional, not empirical.

questions.question: 「原子大部分是空的吗？」按 Carroll 的讲法，这个问题为什么至今没有一致答案？
options: 因为原子核和电子的尺寸至今测不准，无法算出空的部分占多大比例
因为电子在不同元素中的轨道半径差异太大，没有一个适用于所有原子的统一答案
因为卢瑟福散射实验已经证明原子大部分是空的，只是部分物理学家拒绝接受
答案取决于波函数是否代表实在，而物理学家对此没有共识
questions.explanation: Carroll 说，如果你相信波函数代表实在，就不会说原子大部分是空的，而会说它大部分是电子的波函数；但波函数是实在本身还是算概率的工具，物理学家至今没有共识。把问题归结为尺寸测不准，就把一个诠释问题误当成了测量精度问题。
questions.question_en: "Is the atom mostly empty space?" On Carroll's account, why is there still no agreed answer?
options_en: Because the sizes of the nucleus and electron still can't be measured precisely, the empty fraction can't be computed
Because electron orbit radii differ so much across elements that no single answer fits every atom
Because Rutherford's scattering experiment proved atoms are mostly empty, though some physicists refuse to accept it
It depends on whether the wave function represents reality, and physicists don't agree on that
questions.explanation_en: Carroll says that if you believe the wave function represents reality, you wouldn't call the atom mostly empty—it's mostly the electron's wave function; but whether the wave function is reality or a tool for computing probabilities remains unsettled. Blaming imprecise size measurements turns an interpretive question into a question of measurement precision.
